title: The Cheating Trap: Why “Students Will Only Use AI to Cheat” is the Wrong Story
author: Andrew Marcinek
summary: Marcinek challenges the narrative that generative AI is creating a generation of cheaters, placing it alongside earlier panics over calculators, Wikipedia and smartphones. Citing Stanford, Turnitin and survey research, he argues cheating rates have stayed essentially flat since ChatGPT arrived and that AI has changed the method for students who were already cutting corners. He argues students understand the ethics but are confused by inconsistent policies, while employers increasingly expect AI skills, so a school that only hunts cheaters leaves students unprepared. His proposed reframe is from how to catch AI cheating to how to teach AI use while developing students' own capabilities, through visible AI use, teaching limitations, assessing what AI cannot do, and easing the pressures that drive cheating. Bans, he says, only push use underground.
points: Available data suggest cheating behaviour has been roughly stable since ChatGPT, so AI changed the tool of cheating rather than the number of cheaters.
Students largely reject having AI write a whole paper, so the confusion is about policy, not ethics.
Inconsistent teacher rules leave students caught between institutional fear and workplace demand for AI proficiency.
Making AI use visible and teaching its failures, such as fake citations, builds more understanding than secret use.
If an assessment can be completed entirely by AI, that says something about whether it measures what matters.
quotes: Does AI-related academic misconduct exist? Of course. But here’s the uncomfortable truth that research from multiple sources reveals: students who were going to cheat are now using different tools to do it.
Students know the difference between using a tool and letting a tool replace them. They’re not confused about ethics—they’re often confused about policies.

Instead, they’re navigating a landscape where one teacher says AI is cheating, another assigns AI-assisted projects, and their job postings after graduation increasingly list “AI proficiency” as a requirement. We’re creating a generation caught between institutional fear and professional reality.
Someone has to prepare students for this reality. If schools don’t teach students how to use AI thoughtfully, ethically, and effectively, where exactly will they learn it?

Making AI use visible, not hidden. When students can openly discuss how they used AI in an assignment—what prompts they tried, what worked, what failed—they’re learning far more than when they use it secretly and pretend they didn’t.
Pretending it doesn’t exist by banning it entirely just pushes use underground. Assuming it will destroy academic integrity overestimates its novelty and underestimates your students.
Your students are going to use AI. That’s no longer a question. The only question is whether they’ll understand it when they do.
